metadata.title: Educational Data Mining_ Identification of factors associated with school effectiveness in PISA assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for Spain and applies complex-sample weighting in both phases. In the first phase (multilevel models), HLM 7 is used and the authors state that student and school sample weights are necessary to represent the PISA-eligible population; however, they report that student replicate weights could not be used. Instead, they use robust estimators with Huber-White adjustment to compensate for related bias. In the second phase (decision trees in Weka/J48), the authors aggregate student-level predictors to the school level and apply data weighting based on available school sample weights because the school is the unit of analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses the Spanish PISA 2015 sample of 15-year-olds. From the initial 32,330 students and 976 schools, the sample is reduced to 896 schools and 31,236 students by excluding schools with fewer than 20 participants. In phase 1, multilevel models (one per PISA domain: mathematics, reading, science) are estimated using only input variables; schools are then classified as high- or low-effectiveness based on the school-level residuals: high-effectiveness if residuals fall in the first quartile in all three models, and low-effectiveness if residuals fall in the last quartile in all three models. In phase 2, decision trees are trained using a school-level unit of analysis with process predictors aggregated from PISA 2015 context questionnaires, yielding a final analytic subsample of 8,347 students across 239 schools (3,801 high-effectiveness students; 4,546 low-effectiveness students).

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT use outside school for schoolwork

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Spain) — school effectiveness classification (secondary students, aggregated process variables)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Decision tree (J48/C4.5): Training set — TP: 0.906 (high), Precision: 0.929 (high), COR: 0.947 (high), Kappa: 0.849 (global), RRSE: 0.515 (global). Cross-validation (10-fold stratified): TP: 0.837 (high), Precision: 0.884 (high), COR: 0.916 (high), Kappa: 0.747 (global), RRSE: 0.647 (global). Global COR: 0.947 (training) vs 0.916 (CV).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Spain) the study leveraged additional lessons frequency (EXTR_SUBJ), cooperation perceptions (COOPERATE), ICT use outside school for schoolwork (HOMESCH), ICT use outside school leisure (ENTUSE), and weekly lesson minutes (SUBJ_MINS) to predict school effectiveness (high vs low), finding that the decision tree achieved high classification fit (global COR ≈ 0.947 in training and ≈ 0.916 under 10-fold cross-validation; Kappa ≈ 0.849 training and ≈ 0.747 in CV). This indicates that school effectiveness in secondary education can be meaningfully profiled from aggregated process-related context factors, suggesting that education authorities may prioritize monitoring and balancing extracurricular academic load, ICT intensity, and instructional time patterns rather than relying only on socioeconomic inputs, while noting the analysis is cross-sectional and uses aggregated predictors at the school level.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 microdata for Spain (15-year-olds) to build school effectiveness models in two phases. First, multilevel models (one per domain: mathematics, reading, science) use only input variables to estimate school residuals; schools are then labeled high- vs low-effectiveness based on residual quartiles across all three domains. Second, the authors train a decision tree (J48/C4.5) using process variables from PISA 2015 context questionnaires aggregated to the school level, with the unit of analysis being schools. The resulting tree has 25 branches and 13 terminal nodes and shows strong classification performance: global COR ≈ 0.947 in training and ≈ 0.916 in 10-fold stratified cross-validation; Kappa ≈ 0.849 (training) and ≈ 0.747 (CV); RRSE ≈ 0.515 (training) and ≈ 0.647 (CV). The study applies sample weights (student/school weights in HLM; school weights in the tree) and uses robust estimators rather than replicate weights; however, the design is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported, and aggregation may mask within-school heterogeneity.
